title: The Tablighi Jamaat
hook: a worldwide movement of traveling preachers calling Muslims back to prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Deobandi and Barelvi traditions: two mosques on one street, the same school, different ways of showing honor. Your line was two south asian traditions. Which scholar did you read about? Today, a movement that grew out of that same world. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-one.

Late afternoon, a doorbell rings. On the step are a few men you've never seen: one older, one barely out of college, one with a duffel bag over his shoulder. They're not selling anything. They're not collecting money. They've come from another city, and they're sleeping on the floor of the local mosque this week. One of them smiles and says: we're just reminding our brothers about the prayer. Maghrib is at the mosque tonight, there's a short talk after. Will you come? Then they thank you, and walk on to the next door. Today, the people with the duffel bag.
screen: `A DOORBELL, A FEW STRANGERS.` → `NOT SELLING, NOT COLLECTING.` → `WILL YOU COME TO THE PRAYER?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tabligh means conveying, passing the message on. Jamaat means a group. The movement began in Mewat, near Delhi, with a Deobandi scholar named Muhammad Ilyas Kandhlawi, who wanted ordinary Muslims, not only scholars, to carry the basics of faith and prayer to each other. That's the link to yesterday. Second, how it works. Members volunteer to go out, in their own words, in the path of Allah, for a set stretch of time, in small groups. They pay their own way, carry their own bedding, stay in mosques, cook and eat together, and take turns serving each other. In the afternoons, they walk the streets around the mosque, knocking on Muslim doors, inviting people back to the congregation. In the evenings, they read together from collections of virtues and hadith. Third, the ground it stands on. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "And there may spring from you a nation who invite to goodness, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency." And al-Bukhari reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase: convey from me, even if it's a single verse. Tabligh is that conveying, done on foot. Fourth, the shape of it. The movement describes itself as staying out of politics and out of arguments between schools, and as speaking mainly to Muslims, not seeking converts. It has admirers and critics among Muslims. Some praise how it brings people back to the prayer. Some scholars question parts of its reading books, or long absences from home, and members answer those questions in their own terms. Then, in the afternoon, the group goes out again, and knocks.
screen: `TABLIGH: PASSING IT ON.` · `OUT IN SMALL GROUPS, ON FOOT.` · `CONVEY FROM ME, EVEN ONE VERSE.` · `NO POLITICS, MAINLY TO MUSLIMS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn how it works, from the inside. Settle, and breathe. Picture yourself with the duffel bag. A floor to sleep on. Someone else's cooking. A street you don't know, and a door you have to knock on. Notice what comes up. Nerves. Curiosity. Embarrassment. Then picture the other side of the door: someone who hasn't been to the mosque in years, hearing their name said kindly. Sit with both sides. If you pray, you can remember the people who knock and the people who answer. The bell holds the time.
The Tablighi Jamaat. A movement of volunteers who travel in small groups, stay in mosques and knock on doors, calling Muslims back to the prayer. Today's word.

Your line: preaching by traveling. Today, pass one good thing on in person, not by text: a kind word, a reminder, an invitation. Tomorrow, the Salafi approach. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-one.
